clue.text: Legend, very generous sort, Mrs Thatcher — as if!

indicators.note: to sort is to rearrange or put in order, so the letters that follow are to be shuffled

explanation.surface: A sarcastic aside: the famously thrifty Mrs Thatcher as some open-handed figure of legend? As if!
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort' looks like a noun after 'generous', but it is the anagram signal on MRS THATCHER AS IF; the definition is 'Legend, very generous'.
explanation.definitionFit: Santa Claus is a figure of folklore known for bringing presents to every child, so a lavishly giving legend.

clue.text: Insatiable drama queen stood up

indicators.note: in a down clue, standing something up means reading it from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a diva is a temperamental, attention-seeking prima donna

explanation.surface: A demanding diva who has been stood up by a date and remains hungry for attention.
explanation.definitionFit: Avid means greedy or eager to the point of never being satisfied, a close synonym of insatiable.

clue.text: Easily passes with professor coming round

parts.note: to pass something is to hand it on, so passes means hands

indicators.note: the professor's word surrounds the next piece, closing round it

parts.note: a don is a university teacher

explanation.surface: A student sails through an exam once the professor relents and comes round to their view.
explanation.definitionFit: To win hands down is to win without effort, so the phrase is an idiom for easily.

clue.text: Queen's in study endlessly drinking alcohol

definitions.note: Queen's is read as Queen is, the 's being the verb linking definition to wordplay

indicators.note: the study word takes the alcohol inside it, as if swallowing it
without its end, the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: to read a subject is to study it
gin is a spirit

explanation.surface: The monarch is found in her study, taking a drink without stopping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' drops the final letter of the study word; 'Queen's' is Queen is, linking the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Regina is Latin for queen and is the title used after a reigning queen's name, as in Elizabeth Regina.

clue.text: One's appeal right for inspiring artist

indicators.note: to inspire is literally to breathe in, so the word for 'for' takes the rest inside it

parts.note: pro means in favour of, for
one is I, and 's is is: I'S, here IS
SA is short for sex appeal

explanation.surface: Someone's charm is the right thing to inspire a painter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One's' gives I + S, and 'inspiring' puts ISSAR inside PRO.
explanation.definitionFit: Camille Pissarro was a French Impressionist painter, so he is an example of an artist.

clue.text: Increasingly disconcerted by standards in war novel (in more than one way, some might say)

parts.note: more put out, rearranged as a phrase: put out means disconcerted, more means increasingly
a standard is a flag or banner

explanation.surface: Someone growing ever more unsettled by the flags that fill a wartime story.
explanation.walkthrough: The parenthesis admits the stretch: 'put out more' only means 'more put out' if you allow the words to move, and flags also has more than one sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Put Out More Flags is Evelyn Waugh's 1942 novel set in the early months of the Second World War.

clue.text: Declare — Lara heading off after leg bye

indicators.note: the shortened name is placed after the leg side

parts.note: to declare is to say
on is the leg side in cricket

indicators.note: the name loses its heading, its first letter

parts.note: Brian Lara is a famous West Indies cricketer

explanation.surface: Cricket: a declaration as Brian Lara walks off after a leg bye is run.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading off' trims LARA to ARA. A leg bye and a declaration are cricket terms: a run off the batter's body, and a captain ending an innings.
explanation.definitionFit: Sayonara is the Japanese farewell, used in English as a casual goodbye, so it means bye.

clue.text: Wrongly firing Minister without Portfolio at first

indicators.note: the clergyman goes without the next letter, which is removed

parts.note: a minister of religion is a parson

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the following word is wanted

explanation.surface: A cabinet minister with no portfolio is wrongly sacked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minister without Portfolio' looks like the political title, but it is PARSON less P.
explanation.definitionFit: Arson is the crime of deliberately setting fire to property, so it is fire-raising done unlawfully.

clue.text: Brings back some method of control over Washington?

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits over the second

parts.note: reins are used to control a horse, so one rein is some of them
Washington is used for the United States government, the States

explanation.surface: A political question: does Washington restore some form of control?
explanation.definitionFit: To reinstate is to restore someone or something to a former position, to bring it back.

clue.text: 12 flipping thick, Lewis Hamilton now said

indicators.note: flipping turns the word over, so it is read backwards; it also poses as a mild expletive

parts.note: dim means stupid, thick

indicators.note: said means spoken aloud, so we want a word sounding like the title

parts.note: the racing driver was knighted in 2021, so he is now a knight

explanation.surface: An exasperated comment that Lewis Hamilton is being flipping thick about something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipping' turns DIM to MID; 'said' gives NIGHT from KNIGHT. The definition is the number 12, as in twelve o'clock at night.
explanation.definitionFit: Twelve o'clock at night is the hour at which one day turns into the next.

clue.text: Not totally wanton, I'm saying about woman

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the hidden letters are read backwards
only part of these words is used, the answer sitting partly within them

explanation.surface: A speaker says that some woman is not entirely wanton.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not totally' gives NIMSAY inside wantON I'M SAYing, and 'about' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Yasmin is a girl's given name, so a woman can be called this.

clue.text: Initially nervous: when turning to drink, gains a little extra confidence

indicators.note: turning reverses the short word for when

parts.note: as can mean when, as in 'as I left'

indicators.note: only the opening letter of nervous is used
the drink takes in, gains, the next piece

parts.note: Guinness is a brand of Irish stout

indicators.note: a little of extra is just its first letter

explanation.surface: A nervous person finds that turning to drink gives them a little extra confidence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning' reverses the word for when; 'gains' puts the first letter of 'extra' inside the stout, between its two Ns.
explanation.definitionFit: Sanguineness is the state of being sanguine, optimistic and confident about how things will turn out.

clue.text: An oaf at first implying Covid not very problematic — nut!

indicators.note: something problematic is troublesome, so these letters are thrown into disorder
only the opening letter of implying is wanted
the word for very is taken out

explanation.surface: An idiot suggesting that Covid is not much of a problem, an exclamation of contempt at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' removes V from COVID to leave COID; with AN, OAF and I, 'problematic' shuffles the lot.
explanation.definitionFit: A nut is an enthusiast, as in a fitness nut, so a devotee or fan.

clue.text: Shock for a criminal

indicators.note: a criminal arrangement is a wrong one, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A short report: something came as a shock to a criminal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'criminal' rearranges FOR into FRO, which follows A.
explanation.definitionFit: A shock of hair is a thick bushy mass, and an Afro is a hairstyle of that kind.

clue.text: Idiot's taken in twice about countryman

indicators.note: the idiot takes in the next piece, which ends up inside

parts.note: a moron is an idiot; the 's is has, the idiot has taken in
about is abbreviated two ways, C and CA, both from circa

explanation.surface: A fool has been fooled twice over by a man from the country.
explanation.walkthrough: C and CA are both written abbreviations of circa, about.
explanation.definitionFit: A Moroccan is a native of Morocco, so a fellow countryman in that sense.

clue.text: See 1
Awful rubbish! Charlie upset person calling the shots

parts.note: dire means awful

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset turns the pair upside down so they read backwards

parts.note: rot means nonsense, rubbish
Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A critic's outburst at an awful film that has upset somebody named Charlie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns ROT plus C into CTOR.
explanation.definitionFit: A film director gives the orders on set; calling the shots is an idiom for being in charge.

clue.text: Canister could be smaller

indicators.note: the letters could be rearranged into something else, so they are an anagram

explanation.surface: A canister might be smaller than you expect.
explanation.definitionFit: Scantier means more meagre or less ample, so it is a comparative close to smaller.

clue.text: Was sorry about making vulgar sound

indicators.note: making a sound means the vulgar word is spoken aloud and we want its twin in sound

parts.note: rude means vulgar, coarse

explanation.surface: Someone regretted making an embarrassing, vulgar noise.
explanation.definitionFit: To rue something is to regret it, so the past tense fits being sorry about it.

clue.text: Weakness with fellow off sick

indicators.note: the abbreviation for fellow comes off the word, removed from it

parts.note: a failing is a weakness or flaw

explanation.surface: Feeling weak, a fellow goes off sick.
explanation.definitionFit: Ailing means unwell or in poor health, a synonym of sick.

clue.text: Bar staff finally on site dressed as pirates

parts.note: a bar is a counter where drinks are served

indicators.note: only the last letter of staff is wanted
dressing arranges things, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Bar staff turn up at a site in pirate costume for a fancy-dress party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dressed' turns SITE into EITS. 'pirates' is a verb here, not the costume.
explanation.definitionFit: To pirate goods is to copy them illegally, which is to counterfeit or forge them.

clue.text: Labels men as fickle

indicators.note: something fickle changes about, so the letters change their order

explanation.surface: A dismissive generalisation that brands all men as fickle.
explanation.definitionFit: To label someone is to name or call them something, so names is a verb synonym of labels.

clue.text: After not much revision, came top

indicators.note: revision reworks something, and only a slight rearrangement of the letters is needed

explanation.surface: A lazy student who barely revised still came top of the class.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the first two letters of CAME need to swap.
explanation.definitionFit: The acme is the highest point or peak of something, the very top.

clue.text: Lawyer with German's money getting in bother

indicators.note: the money abbreviation gets in between the other pieces

parts.note: a DA is a district attorney, an American lawyer
mit is the German word for with
M is short for money, as in M1 and M2

explanation.surface: A lawyer and some German cash are causing trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with German's' asks for the German word for with; 'getting in' puts the money letter between the lawyer and that word.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild exclamations of annoyance, so the interjection bother is replaced by this curse.

clue.text: One being spiteful about letter going too far

parts.note: A means one

indicators.note: the spiteful word goes around the Greek letter

parts.note: to bitch is to make spiteful remarks
mu is a letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone being nasty about a letter they received has gone too far.
explanation.definitionFit: A bit much is an idiom for excessive or unreasonable behaviour, overstepping the mark.

clue.text: Associates with right-wing types

parts.note: Con is short for Conservative, the right-wing party in Britain
sorts means kinds or types

explanation.surface: Someone who keeps company with right-wing people.
explanation.definitionFit: To consort with people is to keep company or associate with them, often with a hint of disapproval.

clue.text: Close to rock, gets to swim with a seal

indicators.note: swimming letters move about freely, so they are rearranged
the close of a word is its end, so its last letter is wanted

explanation.surface: At the rock's edge, a seal gets into the sea to swim with a companion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to' gives K, the end of 'rock'; 'to swim' mixes it with GETS and A. 'seal' is not the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A gasket is a ring or sheet that seals the joint between two surfaces of an engine or pipe.
